threads.title: The Iran War's Hidden Economic Chain
threads.description: The Hormuz blockade is not just a geopolitical story. It is also the reason the Federal Reserve cannot cut rates even when growth is slowing: energy inflation from the war makes any dovish pivot look irresponsible. Trump started a war that is now constraining the economic policy tools he most wants to use. His two biggest policy priorities are in direct conflict with each other.

connections.relationship: The Hormuz blockade drives a 24% energy price surge that feeds inflation, forcing the Fed to hold rates and making Trump's demand for aggressive rate cuts from his new Fed chair politically toxic.

threads.title: The Mediator Trap
threads.description: Pakistan's mediation role in the Iran ceasefire talks is the only US-Iran diplomatic channel that currently exists. The UAE is punishing Pakistan for it by expelling its workers. But a financially destabilized Pakistan is a worse mediator, not a better-aligned ally. The punishment degrades the tool the US is implicitly relying on, which means the UAE is inadvertently working against the ceasefire the US says it wants.

connections.relationship: UAE deportation of Pakistani workers destabilizes Pakistan's economy and threatens its ability to sustain the mediation role that is currently the only viable channel for a Hormuz ceasefire.

threads.title: The Machine Problem
threads.description: Three stories today involve someone who won the right to govern but inherited a system built by their predecessor to survive their arrival. Magyar faces Orban's judiciary and media apparatus. Warsh walks into a Federal Reserve board packed with dissenting governors who treated his predecessor's final meeting as the most contentious in decades. Democrats face a redistricting machine that SCOTUS just freed from legal constraints. In each case, the question is whether institutional control follows from electoral success or whether the machine outlasts the election.

connections.relationship: In both cases, the outgoing power built institutional barriers (court-packed redistricting maps, a dissenting Fed board) that the incoming winner must navigate without being able to simply undo them.

Orban's Hungary is the advanced case study for what happens when an elected government systematically builds institutional durability against successors; US redistricting machinery is the same strategy in an earlier stage.

threads.title: The Same Vote, Different Results
threads.description: Reform UK surges in local elections while winning only a fraction of council seats. Democrats win the popular vote in dozens of redistricted House races while losing the seats. These two stories involve the same mechanism: electoral systems that translate voter preferences into representation unevenly, amplifying minority preferences into majority power. One is the UK's first-past-the-post; the other is gerrymandered US districts. Both are causing voters to lose faith that their votes produce the governments they voted for.

connections.relationship: Both stories describe electoral systems where the translation of votes into seats systematically under-represents certain voter preferences, eroding confidence that elections produce accountable government.
